soil-bio-276.q: What share of humus do arable soils typically hold?
soil-bio-276.a: On average 2 to 3%, within a range from under 1% to over 12%.

soil-bio-210.q: After a disturbance such as agriculture, how quickly do soil mites recolonise?
soil-bio-210.a: Most recolonise within a few months, but Oribatida take several years.

soil-hist-015.q: In a Winogradsky column, which bacteria use sulfide for photosynthesis, and which tolerate more of it?
soil-hist-015.a: Purple and green sulfur bacteria use it, and green sulfur bacteria tolerate higher sulfide than purple.

soil-bio-223.q: Which fatty acid indicates fungi in a PLFA analysis?

soil-bio-162.q: What happens to plants in sterile soils unless mycorrhizal spores or hyphae are added?
soil-bio-162.a: They often do poorly, because there are no fungi to colonise their roots.

soil-bio-239.q: Who first isolated a microbe from legume nodules, and when?
soil-bio-239.a: Martinus Beijerinck, in 1888, naming it Bacillus radicicola; it is now placed in Rhizobium.

soil-bio-321.q: Do epiphytes draw nourishment from their host?
soil-bio-321.a: No. They use the host only for support and draw no nourishment from it, and they are not rooted in soil.

soil-bio-089.q: What carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is typical of humus?
soil-bio-089.a: Commonly between 8:1 and 15:1, with a median of about 12:1.

soil-bio-090.q: Which organic materials decompose first and quickly, and which persist longest?
soil-bio-090.a: Sugars, starches, simple proteins and organic acids go first and quickly; fats, waxes and resins persist longest.

soil-bio-126.q: Which layers does the term mean in Canada, and what do specialists disagree about?
soil-bio-126.a: In Canada it means the L, F and H horizons; specialists disagree on whether it equals the O horizon or leaves out the litter.

soil-bio-284.q: Why is cellulose hard for most organisms to use, and who manages it?
soil-bio-284.a: Few organisms can metabolize it; some bacteria and protists can, and ruminants and termites use microorganisms to process it.

soil-bio-300.q: What are living and active organic matter?
soil-bio-300.a: Living matter is roots and organisms in the spaces between and inside aggregates; active matter is fresh or partly decomposed residue in the same spaces.

soil-bio-304.q: What happens to extra organic matter once a soil is saturated for its management?
soil-bio-304.a: It stays as lightly protected free particles.

soil-bio-127.q: Why does mor litter decompose slowly?
soil-bio-127.a: Low pH, low nutrients and high lignin, tannin or terpene contents make needle and heath litter slow to decompose.

soil-bio-295.q: How does the rate of organic matter loss change after cropping begins?
soil-bio-295.a: It is rapid in early years, while active organic matter is plentiful, then slows as mainly stable material remains.

soil-bio-303.q: How did water-stable aggregates vary with organic matter and tillage in the New York study?
soil-bio-303.a: The share rose with organic matter and no tillage, from 27% in conventional vegetable soils to 70% in no-till pasture.

soil-bio-298.q: How much wet dairy manure did a Vermont study say was needed yearly under continuous silage corn?

soil-bio-291.q: Why does organic matter pile up at the surface of acid soils?
soil-bio-291.a: Acidity inhibits earthworms, so organic matter is not mixed through the soil layers.

soil-bio-317.q: Which is harder to break down, cellulose or lignin, and why?
soil-bio-317.a: Lignin: it is a network of aromatic components, mainly degraded by fungi, while cellulose breaks into simple sugars that are readily degraded.

soil-bio-288.q: How does organic matter content vary with soil texture?
soil-bio-288.a: Under 1% in sands, 2-3% in loams and 4% to over 5% in clays.

soil-bio-263.q: Which isotope is used most often in stable isotope probing, and why is 15N weaker?
soil-bio-263.a: 13C; 15N gives a weaker DNA density shift because DNA holds fewer nitrogen atoms.

soil-class-011.q: At which level do moisture regime names modify USDA soil names, and what defines aquic soils?
soil-class-011.a: At the suborder level; aquic soils are saturated and almost free of oxygen long enough to show gleying and mottling.

soil-class-020.q: Which soil groups open the WRB key?
soil-class-020.a: Histosols, with thick organic layers, then soils under strong human influence: Anthrosols and Technosols.

soil-class-008.q: How do typic, intergrade and extragrade subgroups differ?
soil-class-008.a: Typic carries the basic concept of its great group; intergrade grades toward another class without being strong enough to place there; extragrade has aberrant properties that keep it out of any other class.

soil-found-101.q: What defines udic soils in USDA soil taxonomy?
soil-found-101.a: They are moist enough year-round in most years to meet plant needs.

soil-class-045.q: How does clay accumulate in an argillic horizon?
soil-class-045.a: Mainly by illuviation, the downward washing of existing clay, with some clay formed in place.

soil-class-042.q: Is the term pedalfer still used in U.S. soil classification?
soil-class-042.a: No, but it survives in college geology texts, and its 'alf' lives on in the name Alfisol.

soil-class-028.q: What happens when flooding comes with soil warmer than about 5 °C?
soil-class-028.a: Microbes use up the oxygen within days and nitrate and ferric oxide are reduced.

soil-class-047.q: How many FAO groups were there originally, and how many in 1988, for Greyzems?
soil-class-047.a: One of the original 26 FAO groups, it remained among the 28 of the 1988 revision.

soil-class-084.q: Why should fill be as free of organic matter as possible?
soil-class-084.a: Decomposing organic matter leaves voids that make the fill settle and can damage structures on it.
